title: The Basic Blueprint: Subject, Verb, Object
brief: Explain that English follows a fixed Subject-Verb-Object (SVO) word order as its default pattern, and that this order is largely non-negotiable in declarative sentences. Define each element (subject as the doer, verb as the action or state, object as the receiver of the action) using original, classroom-ready example sentences such as 'The teacher writes the sentence' and 'My students love grammar.' Contrast English SVO rigidity with the idea that word order carries meaning — show how swapping subject and object changes meaning entirely. Briefly note that not all sentences have an object (intransitive verbs) and give two or three clear examples. This section sets the foundation for everything that follows in the unit.

title: Beyond SVO: Other Sentence Elements
brief: Introduce the elements that extend the basic SVO frame: indirect objects, subject complements, and adverbials. Use original examples to show how a sentence like 'She gave her student a certificate' contains both a direct and indirect object, and how 'He seems tired' uses a subject complement rather than an object. Explain adverbials (time, place, manner, frequency) and show how they can move position in a sentence — 'Every morning, she reviews vocabulary' versus 'She reviews vocabulary every morning' — while the core SVO order stays fixed. Emphasise to the teacher-reader that learners often struggle with adverbial placement and that understanding the stable SVO core helps them see which parts of a sentence are flexible. Keep all examples original and classroom-relevant.

title: Phrases: The Building Blocks Inside Sentences
brief: Define a phrase as a group of words that functions as a single unit but does not contain both a subject and a finite verb. Cover the five main phrase types: noun phrase, verb phrase, adjective phrase, adverb phrase, and prepositional phrase. For each type, provide one or two original example sentences and identify the phrase within them — for instance, 'The very enthusiastic new teacher' as a noun phrase, or 'on the whiteboard' as a prepositional phrase. Explain how phrases slot into the subject, verb, or object positions of the SVO frame, reinforcing the connection to the previous section. Stress the practical classroom value: helping learners recognise phrases prevents them from treating every word as an isolated unit and improves both reading comprehension and writing fluency.

title: Clauses: Main and Subordinate
brief: Distinguish a clause from a phrase by explaining that a clause contains a subject and a finite verb. Define a main clause as one that can stand alone as a complete sentence, and a subordinate clause as one that depends on a main clause for its full meaning. Provide original examples of each — 'The lesson ended' as a main clause, and 'because the bell rang' as a subordinate clause that cannot stand alone. Introduce the most common types of subordinate clause: relative clauses ('the student who answered first'), adverbial clauses ('although she was nervous'), and noun clauses ('I know that he understood'). Explain how subordinating conjunctions and relative pronouns signal the start of a subordinate clause, and note that this is a common stumbling block for learners who produce fragments by writing subordinate clauses as if they were complete sentences.

title: Simple, Compound, and Complex Sentences
brief: Define and clearly distinguish the three core sentence types. A simple sentence contains one main clause and no subordinate clauses — 'The children read quietly.' A compound sentence joins two or more main clauses with a coordinating conjunction (for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so) or a semicolon — 'She explained the rule, and the students practiced it.' A complex sentence contains one main clause and at least one subordinate clause — 'When the activity finished, the teacher collected the worksheets.' Use original examples throughout and show how the same idea can be expressed at each level of complexity. Explain the compound-complex sentence briefly as a combination of both patterns. Emphasise to the teacher-reader that learners at lower levels default to simple sentences and that teaching compound and complex structures explicitly expands their expressive range.

title: Putting It Together: Teaching Word Order in the Classroom
brief: Synthesise the unit by showing how a teacher can use knowledge of SVO order, phrases, clauses, and sentence types as practical classroom tools. Suggest concrete techniques: labelling sentence slots on the board (S / V / O), colour-coding phrases in a written sentence, and asking learners to identify whether a clause is main or subordinate before combining sentences. Provide a short original model sequence — starting with simple sentences, then guiding learners to combine them into compound and complex forms — to illustrate how the grammar concepts in this unit build on each other in a lesson. Remind the reader that accuracy in teacher explanation matters: using precise terms like 'subordinate clause' rather than vague labels like 'extra bit' gives learners transferable metalanguage. Close by noting that a firm grasp of sentence structure underpins the grammar teaching covered throughout the rest of this module.
